analysis.one_liner: Lets states take over all energy development on federal land inside their borders, with no federal environmental review or court challenges.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Energy Committee in June 2013 and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have let any state declare that it will handle energy leasing and permitting on federal land within its borders — land owned by all Americans. Once the federal government certified the state's program, the state would receive the full development rights, and projects would automatically count as meeting federal laws like the National Environmental Policy Act and the Endangered Species Act. The bill went further: no court could review anything done under it. It never moved past the Senate Energy Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Energy companies — particularly oil, gas, and coal firms — would gain the most, since state permitting programs would be faster and friendlier than federal review, and they could not be challenged in court. State governments wanting more energy revenue would also gain, along with any renewable developers seeking faster federal-land approvals.

how_it_helps.text: A state could take over leasing and permitting for all energy development on available federal land within its borders simply by declaring a state program and receiving federal certification.
Once certified, the state would receive all federal rights to develop those energy resources, and state-issued permits would count as fully compliant with federal law.

State-approved projects would be exempt from the National Environmental Policy Act, the Endangered Species Act, the National Historic Preservation Act, the Administrative Procedure Act, and all judicial review.

analysis.who_pays: The public pays: federal lands are owned by all Americans, and the bill removes environmental review, endangered species protection, and the right to challenge projects in court on those lands. Communities near drilling sites, tribal and historic sites outside protected areas, and taxpayers who subsidize cheap extraction would bear the costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public and protected land resources

drawbacks.text: It exempts state-approved energy projects from judicial review entirely, so no court could hear challenges even to an unlawful or harmful project — a nearly unprecedented removal of legal recourse.

It waives the National Environmental Policy Act, the Endangered Species Act, and the National Historic Preservation Act on federal land transferred to state programs, eliminating environmental review, protection for endangered wildlife, and protection of historic sites.

It hands development rights to all forms of energy on available federal land — which belongs to all Americans — to state governments upon a simple declaration, with no federal backstop if the state's rules are weak.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For states wanting faster drilling on federal land, the benefit is real: permitting would move at state speed instead of federal speed, and royalties could support state budgets. The costs fall on the national public: federal lands belong to all Americans, and the bill's ban on judicial review means no court could stop even an unlawful project, and exempting Endangered Species Act review removes the main legal check on harming wildlife. It is a one-way transfer of control with no compensating safeguards.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Energy Committee in June 2013, and the committee never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Senator James Inhofe introduced S. 1233 on June 26, 2013, with 13 Republican cosponsors.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources, where no further action was taken.
The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and expired when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The bill's death preserved federal environmental review, endangered species protections, and citizens' right to challenge federal-land energy projects. Oil, gas, and coal companies lost the chance for faster, challenge-proof federal-land permitting.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal environmental safeguards and public legal rights

for.name: 13 Senate Republicans
for.role: Cosponsors including Sens. Vitter, Paul, Coburn, Crapo, Cruz, Johnson, Lee, Hoeven, Rubio, Cornyn, Risch, Isakson, and Hatch

sides.party_line_note: All 14 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat supported the bill.

industries.note: The bill would let states hand out leases and permits on federal land without federal environmental review, endangered species checks, or court challenges, cutting approval times and legal costs for extractive industries. That cost-shift lands on the public in the form of degraded land, air, and wildlife on land the nation owns.

industries.industry: Wind, solar, and other energy developers
industries.note: The bill covers 'all forms of energy,' so renewable developers would also gain faster permitting on federal land, though the largest beneficiaries are conventional extraction firms.
Interior, Agriculture, and Energy would lose regulatory authority over energy on federal land within participating states, with no mechanism to review or reverse state decisions.
